extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (trademark/patent practitioners), OED/disciplinary counsel, and respondents in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements used to evaluate practitioner misconduct in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (particularly trademark practice), including signature rules, cooperation with investigations, supervision duties, fee division, burden of proof, and sanctioning considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory authority for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admission and to suspend or exclude persons from practicing before it, under 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and 35 U.S.C. § 32; disciplinary hearings are conducted under 37 C.F.R. part 11, subpart C and 5 U.S.C. § 556.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the Office's power to regulate practitioner conduct and to impose discipline; hearings follow Part 11 procedures and ALJs authorized under interagency agreements may preside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and notice requirements (address/update obligations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner must notify the OED Director of the postal address for the practitioner's office and provide written notice of any address change within 30 days (37 C.F.R. § 11.11). Service to the provided address is presumptively effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaints and notices served to the practitioner's §11.11 address (and other reasonably believed addresses) are effective; UPS/mailed delivery records are sufficient to infer receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence of failing to answer the Complaint (default)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer constitutes an admission of the allegations and may result in entry of default judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no Answer is filed within the required time, a decision by default may be entered against the Respondent; the Court may find respondent in default and accept the Complaint's facts as admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must prove alleged disciplinary violations by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is a standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt — evidence must produce a firm belief or conviction as to the truth of the allegations; used to protect liberty interests in disciplinary actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence requiring a signature in trademark matters must bear either (1) a handwritten signature personally signed in permanent ink by the signatory (or a true copy), or (2) an electronic signature that meets the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(c) personally entered by the signatory (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signature rules apply to paper filings, facsimile, TEAS, and ESTTA; declarations are signed under criminal penalty (18 U.S.C. § 1001), so correct signature practice is critical to application integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic signature mechanics and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic signatures must be personally entered by the person named as the signatory, with adopted signature characters placed between two forward slashes per 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(c). Recognized TEAS signature methods include DIRECT (default), ESIGN-ON (hyperlink to third party), and H SIGN (electronic image of handwritten signature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DIRECT requires the signatory to enter signature characters directly; use of ESIGN-ON or H SIGN has distinct procedures; typing another person's electronic signature or having another person enter the keystrokes is not a valid signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP signature guidance (no one may sign for another)
rubrics_metrics.description: TMEP § 611.01(b)–(c) states another person (paralegal, assistant, secretary) may not sign the name of an attorney or other authorized signatory, and typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP emphasizes that manual entry by the identified signatory is required and reiterates regulatory provisions; cites In re Dermahose and In re Cowan as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: TICRS and IP address as objective signature/authenticity evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: TICRS captures when a document was created/submitted via TEAS, the signature method used, and the IP address of the computer used to access TEAS; IP-based geographic data can be used to assess whether a named signatory actually signed in the claimed location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TICRS/IP data can demonstrate discrepancies (e.g., signatures entered from foreign IPs inconsistent with asserted signer location) and are admissible objective indicators of where and how signatures were entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on authorizing others to violate signature rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not allow another to sign trademark applications, declarations, or other filings where the practitioner is the named signatory, nor may a practitioner authorize another to violate USPTO signature rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing assistants to input a practitioner's or applicant's signature violates 37 C.F.R. § 2.193 and TMEP § 611.01(c) and risks invalidation of filings and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of diligence in representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an ethical obligation to act with reasonable diligence in representing a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes taking reasonable steps to ensure filings are signed in accordance with USPTO rules and ensuring client affairs are competently handled; failure can support discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to supervise non-practitioner assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner has ultimate responsibility for ensuring clients' affairs are competently handled and must adequately supervise assistants; inability to shift responsibility to employees absolves the practitioner (case law and prior USPTO orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO has disciplined practitioners for failing to supervise assistants who signed/ filed documents improperly (cites In re Martinez, In re Tachner, In re Meyer, etc.); lack of knowledge of assistant misconduct is not a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cooperate with OED investigations and respond to RFIs
rubrics_metrics.description: During an OED investigation, a practitioner must respond to lawfully issued Requests for Information (RFIs) and cooperate (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)(ii); § 11.801(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond, providing false/misleading information, or withholding documents (without valid privilege log/explanation) is misconduct and an aggravating factor; claims of privacy/confidentiality require explanation or redaction and privilege logs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on submission of false evidence and duty to remediate
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not offer evidence known to be false and, if material evidence is false and known to be so, must take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the USPTO where necessary (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a); § 11.303(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting or failing to correct falsified declarations or signatures threatens trademarks and clients' interests; remediation and disclosure obligations apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee division disclosure and client consent requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If fees are divided or shared with attorneys, a practitioner must describe the fee division arrangements, including amount/percentage allotted to the attorney and whether the applicant consented to the division (including written confirmation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's failure to provide documentation or written client consent for fee divisions was a violation; during RFIs the Office expects contracts, amounts paid, and documentation showing client consent or explanation if none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors for sanctioning (ABA Standards §9.22 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include dishonest or selfish motive; a pattern of misconduct; multiple violations; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders; substantial experience in the practice of law; submission of false evidence; refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct; indifference to restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court applies ABA Standards (e.g., §9.22 subsections) and prior case law to weigh aggravators when determining sanctions; repeated or intentional misconduct increases sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors for sanctioning (ABA Standards §9.32 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors include absence of a prior disciplinary record (STANDARD §9.32(a)) and other factors identified in ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigators may reduce discipline but may be outweighed by serious aggravating factors (e.g., intentional falsity, pattern of misconduct, failure to cooperate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning considerations and applicable rule (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing sanctions, the Court analyzes factors enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) and applies ABA Standards to determine an appropriate sanction (e.g., exclusion, suspension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis weighs the nature of the misconduct, harm to clients/public, aggravating/mitigating factors, and public protection. The decision here concluded exclusion based on the factors listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion/suspension and reinstatement eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded practitioner is barred from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and other matters; an excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of the exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent was excluded; notice references practitioner responsibilities on suspension/exclusion under §11.58 and appeal rights under §11.55 (30 days). Reinstatement requires full compliance with §11.58 conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to participate in disciplinary process as aggravating conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful failure to participate (not answering Complaint, ignoring Orders, not responding to meet-and-confer or default-motion notices) constitutes bad faith obstruction and is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat non-participation as evidence of indifference and contempt for disciplinary procedures and may enhance sanctions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential client injury and public protection rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct such as filing documents with falsified signatures can cause significant potential injury: cancellation of trademarks, loss of enforceability, and harm to clients' proprietary rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The potential for serious client harm supports harsher sanctions to protect the public and integrity of the trademark register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary expectations for RFI/document production (privilege/logs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When OED requests documents (e.g., contracts, compensation records, correspondence), assertions of confidentiality/privacy must be supported with redactions or a privilege log and explanation; blanket privacy claims are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's failure to produce or adequately justify non-production weighed against her; proper responses require either production with appropriate redactions or a legal basis and log for withholding.
